discipline_framing: Judgment and decision science, behavioral economics, and consumer psychology applied to the biases, FOMO, herd mentality, and social proof that drive purchase spikes and trend adoption
audience: Trend analysts, marketers, product and growth teams, and researchers who must explain sudden demand spikes and adoption waves — and audit their own judgment for the same biases
sources: Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow, and the Tversky-Kahneman heuristics-and-biases research program
Gigerenzer's ecological-rationality and fast-and-frugal-heuristics work (the adaptive-heuristic counterpoint)
Cialdini, Influence — social proof, scarcity, commitment, authority, reciprocity, liking, unity
Thaler & Sunstein, Nudge, and the choice-architecture and defaults literature
Banerjee and Bikhchandani-Hirshleifer-Welch information-cascade models of herd behavior
Przybylski-lineage FOMO research and the scarcity/urgency experimental literature (Cialdini's commodity theory roots)
Mathur, Gunawan & Gray et al. on dark-pattern prevalence and regulation, plus the replication-crisis reassessments of priming-era behavioral findings
pitfalls: Treating biases as fixed laws of human nature rather than context-dependent tendencies with contested effect sizes
Ignoring the bias blind spot — assuming consumers are biased while the analyst's own trend calls are objective
Confusing correlation-with-purchase for causal persuasion effects in observed spikes
Sliding from explaining behavior into manipulating it without ethical and legal guardrails
Over-relying on single-study findings from literatures hit by replication failures
